clue.text: Check pub in charge of vicious individuals

parts.note: to bar is to check or block
a bar is a pub
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: Someone checks a pub run by a gang of violent thugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'check' an inspection of the pub; it is a verb meaning block, giving the first of two identical three-letter words.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbaric describes savage, cruel behaviour typical of barbarians, so it fits brutal people as an adjective of character.

clue.text: Judge has sessions reduced

indicators.note: anything reduced is made smaller, so letters are trimmed off the preceding words

parts.note: the word with its first letter cut
the word with its last four letters cut

explanation.surface: A judge finds the court's sitting times cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced' trims both words before it: the head of 'has' and the tail of 'sessions'. 'Judge' looks like the courtroom person but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess something is to evaluate or form an opinion of it, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Member of pack or crew

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a playing card in a deck
second meaning: a sailor, one of a ship's crew

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pack' is a deck of cards here, not a wolf pack; 'crew' is shorthand for a member of a ship's crew, as in jack tar.
explanation.definitionFit: The knave card in each suit carries this name, and it is also an old word for a seaman.

clue.text: Fisherman's position on river

parts.note: an angle is a position or point of view
R is the usual abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Describes where a fisherman stands on the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay; 'on' simply places one piece after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler is someone who catches fish with rod and line, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Crooked looking superior I had reported

parts.note: your superior at work is your boss

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: the contraction of these words is said the same as a word meaning looked at

explanation.surface: Someone says a dodgy-looking superior of theirs had been reported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooked' suggests dishonesty but here describes eyes that do not line up. Boss-eyed is British slang for squinting or cross-eyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Boss-eyed means having a squint or cross-eyed, so the person's gaze looks askew.

clue.text: Speaker's introduction was anxious and fearful

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the very start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
to have cared is to have been worried or concerned

explanation.surface: A speaker introducing a talk feels nervous and frightened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaker's introduction' reads like the opening words of a speech, but it means just the first letter of 'Speaker'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being scared is being frightened or afraid, a plain adjective synonym.

clue.text: Monotonous sound extracted from monotonous instrument

indicators.note: whatever is extracted is pulled out and taken away, leaving the remainder behind

parts.note: humdrum means dull and monotonous
a hum is a low, steady, unvarying noise

explanation.surface: A dreary noise is drawn out of a dull-sounding instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'monotonous' is the trick: the first is part of a phrase for a low drone, the second is a synonym for dull that contains that drone.
explanation.definitionFit: A drum is a percussion instrument, so it is an example of the general category named.

clue.text: Refuse to vote or ban it as ordered

indicators.note: letters that are ordered have been arranged into a new sequence

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A choice in a meeting: don't vote, or ban the motion as instructed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As ordered' reads as 'as instructed', but 'as' belongs to the letters being rearranged and only 'ordered' signals the change.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is deliberately to decline casting a ballot, the formal term for sitting out an election or motion.

clue.text: Gold-plated statuette commending actors in leading parts?

definitions.text: Gold-plated statuette commending actors in leading parts?

parts.words: Gold-plated statuette commending actors in leading parts?
parts.note: surface reading: some ornamental trophy praising performers
setter's reading: the Hollywood prize for Best Actor and Best Actress in a leading role

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading parts' tempts a solver to take the initial letters of the words around it, but nothing spells the answer; the whole clue describes the trophy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette is gold-plated and given to performers in leading roles, among other categories.

clue.text: Bill adopts line offering little hope

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so one piece is taken inside another

parts.note: a bird's bill is its beak
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A man named Bill takes up a pessimistic stance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name or an invoice; it is the bird's mouthpart.
explanation.definitionFit: A bleak outlook is grim and unpromising, with little prospect of improvement.

clue.text: Desire strong drink for five-year period

parts.note: lust is strong desire
rum is a strong spirit

explanation.surface: Craving hard liquor for five years on end.
explanation.walkthrough: An obscure word, built cleanly from two familiar ones; the Latin lustrum was the five-yearly purification after the Roman census.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustrum is a literary term for a span of five years, taken from Roman census practice.

clue.text: Noise indicating contempt for fruit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rude blowing sound made with the tongue and lips
second meaning: a red soft berry

explanation.surface: Someone blows a rude noise at a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude noise is named from rhyming slang, raspberry tart.
explanation.definitionFit: Blowing a raspberry is a derisive noise, and the same word is the red berry grown on canes.

clue.text: Harbingers of death and distressing things overwhelming woman

indicators.note: to overwhelm is to engulf or swamp, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: banes are causes of distress or ruin
she is the pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: Omens of death and other troubles crowding in on a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' is a link word, not part of the wordplay. Banshees come from Irish folklore: female spirits whose wailing foretells a death.
explanation.definitionFit: In Irish legend a banshee's keening warns that someone in the family is about to die.

clue.text: Turn round bad press with little effort

indicators.note: turning something round faces it the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A PR team trying to reverse negative media coverage without much work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad press' looks like a single phrase about media coverage, but 'press' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To dab is to touch lightly and briefly, a gentle pressing motion such as with a cloth.

clue.text: Laid around like this, very much in love

indicators.note: to be around something is to encircle it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: to lay money is to bet, so laid is betted
so means in this way

explanation.surface: Lying about like this, utterly smitten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid' suggests lying down, but it is the gambling sense: to lay a wager.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone besotted is infatuated, so strongly attracted that judgement is clouded.

clue.text: Mock company director to begin with

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: what comes to begin with is at the start, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Making fun of the firm's boss right from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mock' reads as a verb, to ridicule, but here it is the adjective: imitation. Cod is British informal for fake or sham, as in a cod accent.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage cod means imitation or not genuine, matching mock as an adjective meaning sham.

clue.text: Everyone among staff raised money

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something lifts it from bottom to top, so it reads upwards
to be among things is to sit in their midst, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a staff is a rod or stick
everyone is all

explanation.surface: The whole workforce chipped in to raise funds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' suggests employees and 'raised money' fundraising; staff is a stick and 'raised' turns the result upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollar is a unit of currency in Canada, the US and elsewhere, so it is an example of money.

clue.text: State demanding no coverage?

parts.note: surface reading: a country that wants no media attention, or no insurance cover
setter's reading: a condition in which no clothing covers the body

explanation.walkthrough: 'State' suggests a nation and 'coverage' the press; the state is a condition, and the coverage is clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unclothed is a condition of the body without any garments on it at all.

clue.text: Captain disowns son who's out of it

definitions.note: a noun phrase for a person who is asleep

indicators.note: to disown is to reject and cast off, so one letter is thrown out

parts.note: a skipper is a ship's or team's captain
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A captain disowns a son who is completely wasted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of it' suggests drunk or dazed; here it means asleep. To kip is British slang for to sleep, so a kipper is a sleeper (and also a smoked herring).
explanation.definitionFit: A kipper here is one who kips, informal British for someone who is sleeping and unconscious to the world.

clue.text: Former English MP last in parliament not subject to tax

parts.note: ex means former
E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

indicators.note: the last in a word is its final letter, so only that end letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A former English member of parliament, the last in the house, escapes taxation.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one politician's story; each word is a separate piece. An MP is a Member of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Exempt means freed from an obligation, and tax-exempt income or goods owe no duty.

clue.text: Ring work about hotel porter from US

parts.note: to ring is to bell, or a bell rings
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone rings for service at a hotel and a porter arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' here means concerning, loosely joining the pieces; the hotel letter actually comes before the work, so do not try to put one inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: In American hotels a bellhop carries guests' luggage, the equivalent of a British hotel porter.

clue.text: Singer hosted by ambassador

indicators.note: a guest hosted by someone is held within their house, so the letters sit inside the next word

parts.note: letters two to five of the word

explanation.surface: A singer is entertained at an embassy reception by the ambassador.
explanation.walkthrough: The singer is not a guest; the letters are tucked inside the diplomat's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass is a male vocalist with the lowest range, so the word names a kind of singer.

clue.text: Fish had strong aroma

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small silvery food fish
second meaning: gave off an odour, past tense

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a complaint about a pungent fish; the two halves are separate meanings, the second the British past tense of a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The small silvery fish shares its name with the British past tense of the verb for giving off an odour.

clue.text: Only down-to-earth part of Oxford?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: single, one and only
second meaning: the underside of a shoe, which touches the ground

explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' is not the university city but a style of lace-up shoe, and 'down-to-earth' is taken literally: the part that meets the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means only or single, and also names the bottom surface of a shoe that touches the floor.

clue.text: Catherine's cycling to move round easily?

indicators.note: cycling goes round in a loop, so a letter moves from one end to the other

parts.note: Kate is short for Catherine, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: Catherine takes to her bike to get around easily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests a bike ride; it is the instruction to move the final letter round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To skate is to glide smoothly over ice, and figuratively to get through something with ease.

clue.text: Coverage of The Sun including Liberal in misguided pieces

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other letters
something misguided has gone astray, so these letters are jumbled out of their proper order

parts.note: taken as written, letters to rearrange
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: The Sun newspaper's reporting includes a Liberal in some ill-judged articles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Sun' looks like the British tabloid newspaper and 'coverage' its reporting; the sun here is the star, and coverage is the moon blocking it.
explanation.definitionFit: A solar eclipse happens when the moon passes in front of our star and hides it from view.
